content: Rilpivirine can increase the toxicity of erythromycin ethylsuccinate by prolonging the QTc interval. Caution and monitoring are advised when these drugs are co-administered. Similarly, rilpivirine should be used cautiously with any drug that carries a known risk of Torsades de Pointes. Erythromycin lactobionate can elevate rilpivirine levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism, necessitating careful monitoring. Rilpivirine also increases the toxicity of erythromycin lactobionate via QTc prolongation, requiring caution. Rilpivirine can increase the toxicity of escitalopram by prolonging the QTc interval, and escitalopram can similarly increase rilpivirine toxicity. Famotidine reduces rilpivirine levels by increasing gastric pH, which can lead to treatment failure or resistance. Famotidine should be administered at least 12 hours before or 4 hours after rilpivirine. Co-administration of rilpivirine with fingolimod, flecainide, or fluconazole can increase QTc prolongation risks, and caution is advised. Fluconazole also raises rilpivirine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism, but no rilpivirine dose adjustment is required. Rilpivirine increases the toxicity of fluoxetine, fostemsavir, gemifloxacin, and haloperidol by prolonging the QTc interval. Fostemsavir, at higher doses, has been associated with QTc prolongation, and close monitoring is recommended. Drugs like hydroxyzine, ibutilide, iloperidone, and indapamide, when co-administered with rilpivirine, also increase QTc prolongation risks, necessitating caution. Indinavir and isoniazid elevate rilpivirine levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring monitoring. Itraconazole increases rilpivirine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism, but no dose adjustment is needed. Both drugs can prolong the QTc interval, requiring caution. Ketoconazole has similar effects on rilpivirine levels, and fungal infections should be monitored when azole antifungals are co-administered. Rilpivirine increases the toxicity of lapatinib, levofloxacin, and lopinavir by prolonging the QTc interval. Lopinavir also raises rilpivirine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Magnesium-containing compounds (e.g., magnesium chloride, magnesium gluconate, magnesium oxide, magnesium sulfate) decrease rilpivirine levels by increasing gastric pH, potentially reducing its efficacy. Antacids should be administered at least 2 hours before or 4 hours after rilpivirine. Rilpivirine increases the toxicity of maprotiline, moxifloxacin, and nilotinib by prolonging the QTc interval. Nefazodone and nelfinavir elevate rilpivirine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring monitoring. Nizatidine reduces rilpivirine levels by increasing gastric pH, which may lead to treatment failure or resistance. H2 antagonists should be administered at least 12 hours before or 4 hours after rilpivirine. Rilpivirine increases the toxicity of nortriptyline, octreotide, and ofloxacin by prolonging the QTc interval. Orlistat decreases rilpivirine levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption, potentially leading to virological failure in HIV patients. HIV RNA levels should be monitored, and orlistat discontinued if viral load increases. Osilodrostat, ozanimod, and paliperidone, when co-administered with rilpivirine, increase QTc prolongation risks, requiring close monitoring. Pazopanib, pentamidine, and pimozide also exhibit similar risks when combined with rilpivirine. Posaconazole increases rilpivirine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism, but no dose adjustment is needed. Both drugs can prolong the QTc interval, necessitating caution. Potassium chloride decreases rilpivirine levels by increasing gastric pH, potentially reducing its efficacy. Antacids should be administered at least 2 hours before or 4 hours after rilpivirine. Rilpivirine increases the toxicity of procainamide, propafenone, and protriptyline by prolonging the QTc interval. Quetiapine, quinidine, and quinine also exhibit similar risks when co-administered with rilpivirine. Quizartinib and rilpivirine both increase QTc prolongation risks, requiring close monitoring with ECG. Rilpivirine increases the toxicity of ranolazine and risperidone by prolonging the QTc interval. Ritonavir elevates rilpivirine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism, and rilpivirine increases ritonavir toxicity via QTc prolongation. Romidepsin, selpercatinib, and sertraline also exhibit QTc prolongation risks when combined with rilpivirine. Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate decreases rilpivirine levels by increasing gastric pH, potentially reducing its efficacy. Drugs with pH-dependent solubility should be administered at least 2 hours before or after sodium zirconium cyclosilicate. Solifenacin and sotalol, when co-administered with rilpivirine, increase QTc prolongation risks, requiring caution. Sunitinib, tacrolimus, and telavancin also exhibit similar risks when combined with rilpivirine. Rilpivirine increases the toxicity of thioridazine and thiothixene by prolonging the QTc interval. Tipranavir elevates rilpivirine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism, but rilpivirine does not affect protease inhibitor concentrations. Toremisene and trimipramine also exhibit QTc prolongation risks when co-administered with rilpivirine. Trimagnesium citrate anhydrous decreases rilpivirine levels by increasing gastric pH, potentially reducing its efficacy. Antacids should be administered at least 2 hours before or 4 hours after rilpivirine. Ublituximab reduces rilpivirine efficacy through immunosuppressive effects, increasing infection risks. Valbenazine and vandetanib, when co-administered with rilpivirine, increase QTc prolongation risks, requiring caution. Voclosporin and rilpivirine both increase QTc prolongation risks, necessitating close monitoring. Voriconazole elevates rilpivirine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism, but no dose adjustment is needed. Both drugs can prolong the QTc interval, requiring caution. Vorinostat and ziprasidone also exhibit QTc prolongation risks when combined with rilpivirine. Chloroquine increases rilpivirine toxicity via QTc prolongation, though the significance is unclear. Crizotinib and rilpivirine both increase QTc prolongation risks, though the significance is also unclear. Adagrasib and rilpivirine should generally be avoided due to additive QTc prolongation effects, which may increase the risk of Torsades de Pointes and other serious arrhythmias. If co-administration is unavoidable, close monitoring is recommended. Albuterol, alfuzosin, and aluminum hydroxide, when co-administered with rilpivirine, require close monitoring due to QTc prolongation risks or reduced rilpivirine levels. Amiodarone, amisulpride, and amitriptyline also exhibit QTc prolongation risks when combined with rilpivirine. ECG monitoring is recommended for amisulpride. Amoxapine and anagrelide should generally be avoided due to significant QTc prolongation risks. Apomorphine, arformoterol, and aripiprazole, when co-administered with rilpivirine, require close monitoring due to QTc prolongation risks. Arsenic trioxide and artemether also exhibit similar risks, with artemether generally requiring an alternative drug. Asenapine and its transdermal form, when combined with rilpivirine, necessitate close monitoring due to QTc prolongation risks. Aspirin/citric acid/sodium bicarbonate decreases rilpivirine levels by increasing gastric pH, potentially reducing its efficacy. Antacids should be administered at least 2 hours before or 4 hours after rilpivirine.
